Agreed 2026-09-04. **Nothing here is built.** This records the shape and the
reasoning so the decisions are not re-litigated, and so whoever implements it
knows which parts are settled and which are still open.

Supersedes the sketch in `monetization-direction` (session memory), which had
the meter as shopping trips alone.

---

## The shape, in one paragraph

Every feature is available to everybody. The free tier differs only in **how
much** you may do, expressed as **allowances** that visibly decrement. The user
is told where they stand before they run out, so hitting a limit is the end of a
countdown they were watching rather than a door slammed in their face. Paying
lifts the limits. Nothing is ever removed from an account that already has it.

---

## Settled

### No ads

Rejected, and the reasoning generalises: sessions are seconds long and this is a
shared family utility. There is no attention here to sell. The same argument
constrains our own messaging — see *The nudge* below.

### No feature gating

Every capability — camera, dictation, aisle mapping, all of it — works on the
free tier. A crippled free tier is what people judge the app on, and the AI is
the part that makes anyone want to pay for it. Gate the volume, never the
feature.

### A timed trial was considered and rejected

"Free for 30 days, then locked" takes the app away. An allowance never does: the
app keeps working, just less. People tolerate a smaller app far better than a
dead one, and a household grocery list that stops working strands two people
mid-week, not one.

### Two kinds of limit, presented separately

The status screen has two sections, and the difference is in the heading rather
than left to be inferred:

| Section | Heading reads | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Recurring** | "Resets in 12 days" | AI mapping calls, shopping sessions |
| **Structural** | "Lifts when you subscribe" | Household members, photos per item, total items and suggestions |

"12 AI calls left this month" and "1 member slot left" look identical on a screen
and mean entirely different things — one refills on its own and one never will.
Labelling them the same way means people wait for the wrong number to reset.

The structural section doubles as the upgrade pitch: it is a list of exactly what
subscribing unlocks, sitting where somebody is already looking at their limits.

### Entitlement is per household, not per person

One member subscribes, the receipt is validated, and the **household** is marked
entitled on `householdId`. Every member benefits. This sidesteps Apple's
multi-user problem without Family Sharing.

Consequence for the copy: whoever hits a limit may not be whoever pays. The
message has to make sense to a person who cannot buy — "your household is out of
placements this month" — while offering the purchase to the person reading it.

---

## The nudge

**The hard rule: never while `shoppingStatus == AT_STORE`.**

The app already distinguishes list-building at home from standing in a shop.
Asking somebody for money mid-shop is the one moment that turns a limit into
being held hostage, and it is the fastest way to make a household utility feel
predatory. This is an invariant, enforced in one place, not a judgement call at
each call site.

**Where it does appear:** on launch, when the app has been idle a while, as a
status summary — where you stand across every allowance.

**Open, and worth settling before building:**

- **Frequency.** This app is opened several times a day to add one thing. Every
  launch is too often; the recommendation is at most once a day, and only past
  some fraction of the allowance. Early in the month the number is noise.
- **Form.** A pop-up must be dismissed, which taxes every launch. A line under
  the list header costs nothing to ignore and is read by the same people. Not
  settled — he leans toward the pop-up on launch, which is defensible *because*
  it is bounded to launch rather than following you around.

**Why forewarning is the whole mechanism.** People resent surprise more than
restriction. An allowance that has been counting down in plain sight for a
fortnight is a fact; the same wall with no warning is an ambush. The reminders
are not marketing, they are what makes the limit acceptable.

---

## The allowances

**"Allowance" is the word, everywhere** \u2014 in the code, in the UI and in this
document. Not "restriction", not "limit", not "quota". An allowance is something
you have; a restriction is something done to you, and the difference is the whole
tone of the free tier.

Numbers below are provisional. They are reasoning, not measurements — see the
warning under *The economics*.

| Allowance | Kind | Provisional | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI mapping calls | Recurring | — | The only line with real marginal cost |
| Shopping sessions | Recurring | — | Understandable unit; see the caveat below |
| Household members | Structural | **2** | Two people shop in most households, so it rarely bites; the third is a genuine reason to pay |
| Total items | Structural | **50** | List and suggestions together — see below |
| Photos per item | Structural | — | S3 is charged per GB; a real cost, unlike sessions |

### One item allowance, not two

There is no separate suggestions cap, because there is no separate list.
`GroceryItem` is a single table with a status — `ACTIVE`, `IN_CART`,
`SUGGESTION` — and items move between them. The shopping list and the
suggestions are two views of one pool.

So the allowance is **total items in the household**, and it covers both by
construction. A suggestions cap smaller than the item cap would be incoherent
anyway: everything in suggestions arrived there from the list.

It also behaves like every other allowance — the wall refuses the next add, and
the user makes room by deleting. Nothing falls off on its own and nothing is
discarded behind their back.

### Comping an account

There must be a way to lift a household's allowances by hand, with no purchase —
friends, testers, people who helped. A flag on `Household` set by the admin
tooling, separate from any receipt, so the entitlement check reads
`subscribed || comped`.

Worth building at the same time as the paywall rather than after it: it is how
every allowance gets tested against a real account without buying anything.

### Two warnings carried forward from earlier decisions

**A shopping session is not an outing.** One trip to two shops finishes two
sessions — observed 2026-08-30, and correctly recorded as two. A household may
run 3–4 a week, not 1–2. Any cap has to be set against that, or it bites the
normal case in the first week.

**A tight member cap was rejected on 2026-09-03, and reinstated on 2026-09-04.**
The original objection: a family of four is exactly who wants a shared list, and
a cap of two stops them experiencing why they would pay. The counter, which
carried: two people shop in most households, so a cap of two rarely bites at all,
and the third person is a clear and honest reason to pay rather than an
artificial one. It remains a poor *cost* proxy — five people shopping twice a
month cost less than two shopping daily — so it is sold as capacity, not as
metering.

### The wall must never eat work in progress

Hitting a limit refuses the **next** action. It never discards something
half-done, and it never fails a save that was already accepted. That is the
difference between a limit and a bug, and it is the one way this design could
make the app feel broken.

---

## Implementation notes

### Two kinds of count

| Allowance | How it is known |
|---|---|
| Total items | **Derived.** Query `groceryItemsByHouseholdIdAndStatus` with `Select: COUNT` |
| Household members | **Derived.** Query `usersByHouseholdId` with `Select: COUNT` |
| AI mapping calls | **Must be accumulated.** Not recorded anywhere today |
| Shopping sessions | **Must be accumulated.** Not recorded anywhere today |

Query the GSIs, never scan the table: a scan reads every household's rows to
count one household's, and it gets slower and dearer as the app grows.

### The two that need building

Neither of these leaves a row today.

**Shopping sessions.** `Household` carries `shoppingStatus`, `activeShopperId`,
`shoppingStoreId` and `shoppingStartedAt` — all *current state*, overwritten by
the next session. `CommitAction` has eight values and none of them is starting or
finishing one. A completed session is invisible the moment it ends.

**AI calls.** They exist only as CloudWatch log lines, which cannot answer "how
many this month" per household at request time.

Simplest shape for both: counters on `Household` — `aiCallsThisPeriod`,
`sessionsThisPeriod`, `periodStartedAt` — incremented with an atomic DynamoDB
`ADD` inside the Lambda that does the work, and reset lazily when
`periodStartedAt` has rolled past the period. No scheduled job, no cron.

### Metered per household, attributed per user

Entitlement is per household, so the allowance is a **shared household pool**.
Metering per user would give a two-person household double the allowance and let
one member run dry while the other had plenty — of one shared list.

Record *who* spent each call as a telemetry field, not as a separate budget. It
answers "is one person doing all the mapping" without turning the pool into two.

### Enforcement is server-side

The client check keeps the UI honest; the Lambda refusing is what makes the
allowance real. `inferProductAisle` already calls `requireHousehold`, which is
where the AI check belongs — same function, same place, one more reason to
refuse.

A client-only check is not a limit, it is a suggestion.

## The economics

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not plan against these numbers

Every figure below comes from **two developers testing the app**, on the day the
telemetry shipped. It is not usage data. It is skewed in both directions at once:

- **AI is overstated.** Most of those calls were deliberate mapping runs against
  a store built minutes earlier, to exercise the feature. Nobody shopping behaves
  like that.
- **AI is also understated.** A real new household maps a full store's worth of
  items over its first weeks; ours had sixteen.
- **Amplify is wildly overstated.** \$2.71 of build minutes is a dozen deploys in
  one afternoon, and has nothing to do with users at all.

What the numbers are good for is **shape** — which line dominates, and by roughly
what order of magnitude. AI being ~20x the infrastructure is a conclusion worth
carrying; \$0.58 a month is not.

**Real data needs real users.** A fortnight of a handful of households who are
actually shopping, from the structured events now being logged. Until then, treat
every figure here as an illustration of the argument, not as an input to a price.
:::

Measured 2026-09-04 from the telemetry shipped the same day.

| | |
|---|---|
| `inferProductAisle` | 3 calls, 34 products mapped, **\$0.035** |
| Cost per product mapped | **~\$0.001** |
| Extrapolated to 49 calls/month | ~\$0.58 per household per month — *see the warning above* |
| AWS, whole account | \$3.19/month |
| Cognito | Free to 10,000 MAU — see `APP-STORE-READINESS.qmd` |

**Output tokens exceeded input** — 1,983 against 1,898. Output is 5x the price of
input on Sonnet, so **more than half the AI bill is the `reasoning` prose**, the
"Pasta sauce is typically shelved alongside pasta…" sentence that most people
never read.

### Pull the cost levers before setting a price

Both are code changes with no user-visible downside, and together they plausibly
move the number by an order of magnitude — to well under \$0.10 per household per
month.

1. **`inferProductAisle` from Sonnet to Haiku.** Output drops from \$15 to \$5
   per Mtok. Do it in the same pass as the Bedrock migration; they rewrite the
   same model-id lines in the same handlers.
2. **Trim or drop `reasoning`,** at least for high-confidence results.

Pricing decided against today's cost is pricing against a number about to be
invalidated.

### What the infrastructure actually costs

Real bill, 30 days to 2026-09-04, by service:

| Service | 30 days |
|---|---|
| AWS Amplify | **\$2.71** |
| AppSync | \$0.028 |
| CloudWatch | \$0.001 |
| Lambda | \$0 |
| DynamoDB, S3, Cognito | not billed |

**The \$2.71 is not a user cost.** Amplify bills build minutes — it is what
*deploying* costs, and it scales with how often `main` is pushed, not with how
many households exist. On a day of heavy iteration it dominates the bill and
says nothing about users.

Everything users actually touch came to **\$0.03 a month**. Cognito is free to
10,000 MAU, Lambda and DynamoDB did not register at this volume.

So per household: **AI \$0.58, infrastructure \$0.03** — AI is roughly 20x
everything else combined, and at 100x the users the ratio holds, because nothing
else on the bill grows fast enough to matter.

**The corollary that shapes the free tier: a household that never touches AI
costs essentially nothing.** Be generous with everything that is not an AI call;
the entire monetization question reduces to metering that one thing.

### The cost asymptotes, it does not just front-load

A new household has an empty list, no suggestions and no stores. All three fill
and then **plateau**: the suggestion list converges on what this household
actually buys, the store list stops growing at the two or three shops they use,
and — because those two are finite — the aisle mappings saturate. Once a
household's regular items are placed in its regular stores, inference has nothing
left to do.

So AI spend per household decays toward zero with tenure. A mature household
costs storage and API calls, which is the \$0.03 above.

**This inverts the usual assumption, and it matters for choosing numbers.** The
expensive user is not the heavy user, it is the *new* user. A long-tenured
household that shops daily costs less than a fortnight-old one that shops weekly.

**Consequence for a recurring AI allowance:** it binds hardest in month one and
stops binding by month three. That is backwards — the meter would be tightest
exactly when somebody is still deciding whether the app is any good, and slack
once they are committed and costing nothing. Worth deciding deliberately how to
handle this rather than discovering it:

- a larger allowance for a household's first month, or
- a lifetime onboarding allowance separate from the recurring one, or
- accept it, on the grounds that hitting the wall while enthusiastic is exactly
  when somebody is most willing to pay.

The third is a real position, not a cop-out — but it should be chosen, not
stumbled into.

### The shape of the cost is front-loaded

Mapping a store is most of the spend and it happens in week one; a settled
household costs almost nothing. Revenue metered on recurring allowances is flat.
So the loss is on a household that onboards heavily and churns, and the margin is
on one that stays. Normal enough, but it means **the free tier's real exposure is
churn, not heavy use** — and that a generous free tier is affordable, because
most free households cost pennies after their first fortnight.

---

## Open questions

- Price points. \$0.99 to finish out the month was the original sketch; at 15%
  App Store commission that nets \$0.84, which is comfortable against \$0.10 and
  thin against \$0.58. Settle after the cost levers.
- Subscription price and period.
- Every allowance number.
- Nudge frequency and form (above).
- Whether a household that lapses keeps its data — it must, but the read-only
  behaviour needs specifying.

## Prerequisites

- Per-household authorization — **done**, verified with an outsider account.
- Cost per household — **now measurable**; the telemetry landed 2026-09-04.
  A fortnight of data turns the estimate above into a number.
- Receipt validation and the entitlement flag on `Household` — not started.
